Yogender Kumar 3w Report this post Tech hiring sometimes feels like a game with rules that keep changing. You build AI projects. “We need cloud skills.” You learn cloud technologies. “We need practical experience.” You complete internships. “We need open-source contributions.” You finally build a portfolio with everything they asked for. “We've decided to move forward with other candidates.” At some point, you have to wonder: What exactly does it take to get hired? Behind the humor is a real problem with how technical talent is evaluated. Candidates are constantly told to learn more, earn more certifications, build more projects, and gain more experience. But the goalpost keeps moving. Here is what hiring teams often overlook: A candidate doesn't need to know everything. They need to demonstrate that they can learn, solve problems, and deliver results. A strong technical profile tells a story. → Projects show how you solve real problems. → Certifications demonstrate structured learning. → Internships provide exposure to professional environments. → Open-source contributions reveal how you collaborate. → Experience shows how you've applied your skills in practice. The real value comes from understanding what a candidate can actually do with what they've learned. And for job seekers, there's another important lesson. Don't spend years collecting certificates while waiting to feel qualified enough. Build something. Document your work. Improve your resume. Apply consistently. And don't limit your job search to LinkedIn. Here are useful websites to help you find remote opportunities and manage your job search: 1. Remote Rocketship Explore remote opportunities from companies hiring worldwide. https://lnkd.in/gXikkG8i 2. Remotive Discover curated remote jobs, particularly in tech. https://lnkd.in/d8yRt6FQ 3. Eztrackr Build your resume and track your job applications in one place. https://lnkd.in/gTnZ6Csf Focus on the skills that matter, demonstrate your abilities through real work, and keep putting yourself out there. The best hiring process identifies potential and ability, not just the candidate with the longest checklist. What's more valuable in tech hiring: a perfect resume or proof that you can solve real problems? Taruf Ali 2w Report this post The entry-level tech job market has changed, and new developers need to adapt. In the US, employment for software developers aged 22–25 has dropped nearly 20% since late 2022 (Stanford Digital Economy Lab). Most new hiring is going to experienced engineers, and juniors are now expected to do what mid-level engineers did a few years ago. But here’s the other side: talent is no longer limited by location. Remote work and freelance platforms mean a skilled developer anywhere can work with teams across the world. The traditional entry door is narrower, but the global one is wider than ever. From my own work in QA automation, one thing stands out: teams don’t just want people who can write code. They want people who can prove it works, find where it breaks, and keep it secure. That mindset is what’s pulling me toward cybersecurity. What this means for students and early-career developers: 🔹 Don’t wait for a job posting. Land your first paid project, even a small one, before you graduate. 🔹 Build one real, deployed project with users rather than ten tutorial apps. 🔹 Learn to work with AI tools, not around them. Interviews now test this. 🔹 Specialize: security, cloud, data, QA automation, or AI engineering. 🔹 Make your work visible on GitHub and LinkedIn. A degree opens the conversation. Proof of work closes it. To the experienced professionals in my network 👇 Looking back at your early career, what’s one piece of advice you wish someone had given you? A few words from you could make a real difference for someone just starting out. Anmol Jasan 3w Report this post My job filter marked a listing "not open to India". The post itself says it's only for people living in India. On 26 September my script pulled 699 remote job listings for AI, Python and automation work. 196 passed my filter. It trusted each job board's location field, and that field said 22 of them were open to someone in India. Then I read the descriptions themselves. → 127 of the 167 that had any text never say where you can live. The board's field is all you get. → When they do say, the field is wrong in both directions. One listed as "Anywhere in the World" says "US based applicants only". One listed as "United States" says, in capitals, that it's "only available to individuals living in India". My filter had ranked it 155th of 196. → 6 of the 10 posts that give working hours put at least two of them between 10 PM and 7 AM in India. → 3 of the "jobs" were courses. One says it "does not include salary, employment, internship placement, or job guarantee." So I turned that reading into a tool. Paste a job post, pick where you live, and it shows the lines that decide it: where you can live, the hours in your own time zone, whether pay is listed, and anything that asks you to pay them. The part I'd rather leave out: my first versions misread 15 lines and missed 3. "Collaborators based all around the world" is not a hiring policy. "R$6,600" is Brazilian reais, not dollars. Each mistake is now a test, and they're all listed on the receipts page. No AI inside. It runs in your browser, and nothing you paste is uploaded.
